A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SafetyAnalyst research. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison, and renamed components and relocated material can be matched. Internal reporting inconsistencies affect particular judgments rather than material completeness.

before.justification: v1 reports original SafetyReporter classification results in Tables 2–3, generated-feature statistics, and a human evaluation involving 126 annotators in Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 reports original classification and human-evaluation results, alongside new feature ablations, SORRY-Bench category analyses and inference-time measurements.

M1.justification: The paired specialist LMs, harm-benefit trees and weighted aggregation remain. However, v1 specifies 29 parameters with separate harmful/beneficial immediacy discounts; v2 specifies 28 while Figure 3 still displays 29 weights, including both discounts. The PDFs do not resolve whether the aggregation procedure changed or its documentation became inconsistent.

E1.justification: Training sources remain WildJailbreak, WildChat and AegisSafetyTrain. The SimpleSafetyTests, HarmBench, WildGuardTest, AIR-Bench and SORRY-Bench evaluations are retained. New breakdowns and the case study analyze existing coverage; the broader AI-behavior framing introduces no evaluated task.

E2.justification: v1 Table 3 and v2 Table 2 contain the same OpenAI moderation, Llama-Guard, Aegis-Guard, ShieldGemma, WildGuard and GPT-4 comparators. The new diagnostic comparisons reuse existing baselines; Appendix C.1 expands their descriptions without adding methods.

E3.justification: Reported adversarial training augmentation increases from 6,368 to 13,838 prompts. v2 also introduces feature-permutation ablation protocols, category-wise accuracy analysis and latency testing. These substantially extend the experimental design, while retained benchmark sizes and weighted-F1 averaging remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds SORRY-Bench failure analysis by prompt category and seven feature-ablation conditions on WildGuardTest and WildJailbreak (Appendix C, Figure 4 and Table 5). Appendix E adds a phishing-prompt classification case study with proposed steering adjustments. These analyses have no counterparts in v1.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for classification results. The new ablations provide point estimates without uncertainty estimation. The human-study participant counts and agreement-rate calculation are retained.

E6.justification: For the revised training configuration, v2 Table 2 reports weighted F1 of 81.2, replacing 75.4 in v1 Table 3. SimpleSafetyTests changes from 95.2 to 88.8 and SORRY-Bench from 69.1 to 75.4. Student validation scores, feature statistics and learned weights also change, and new latency, ablation and category-level results are added. Baseline scores and human-agreement results are retained.

T1.justification: Both retain the taxonomies and weighted-sum formulation, with no theorems or proofs. v2 rewrites the aggregation and optimization expressions, but its 28-parameter specification conflicts with the 29 weights in Figure 3. This prevents reliably distinguishing a substantive mathematical revision from restatement or documentation error.

C1.justification: v1 presents a framework for LLM content safety moderation. v2's title, abstract, contributions and conclusion broaden the framework to safety moderation of AI behavior generally, treating LLM prompt classification as one implementation. This substantially expands claimed applicability, although the evaluated task remains unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 attributes GPT-4's SORRY-Bench advantage to cipher handling, interprets the ablations as showing greater importance of harms and likelihood, and qualifies these findings as potentially dataset-dependent. It also makes latency-based applicability and misuse of steerability more explicit. The central cost-benefit and pluralistic-alignment interpretations remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies 500 alignment prompts, 300 validation-test prompts, frozen inference weights, the H>0 classification rule, and batched vLLM evaluation on one H100. It omits v1's explicit Llama-70B training-data downsampling statement. These are changes in reproducibility documentation; newly disclosed details alone do not establish changed settings.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens positioning toward AI-behavior safety, adding literature on agents, governance, red-teaming, privacy, security and alignment, plus DICES and PRISM. It removes the dedicated symbolic-knowledge-distillation review and associated Jung, Tang and Xu references. The claimed novelty of the effect taxonomies remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method and related-work narratives are extensively rewritten. SafetyReporter is largely renamed SafetyAnalyst; v2 introduces explicit Contributions and Additional Benefits sections, reorganizes the discussion into the conclusion, and reorders and expands the appendices.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, reorders and enlarges the tree/framework figures, redraws the weight display, and relocates descriptive and human-evaluation tables. It adds the SORRY-Bench category chart and ablation table. The human-annotation interface image is retained and resized.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's aggregate evaluations, v2 adds useful feature ablations, benchmark failure analysis, measured inference costs and clearer evaluation details. These improve scrutiny and practical interpretation. The gain is limited by inconsistent aggregation specifications and a steering example that proposes, rather than measures, adjusted outcomes; higher reported F1 alone does not establish a substantial overall improvement.
